Ithaca.wildlife_intro:
Ithaca keeps our crew busy with Norway rats in the rental blocks, raccoons and squirrels off the gorge canopy, and groundhogs on the hillside lots. Cayuga Lake  gives wildlife food, water, and cover within a short run of almost every roof in town, and the housing does the rest — once an animal finds a soft soffit, an uncapped chimney, or a gap at the roofline, it treats the house as part of its territory.

The year has a rhythm in Ithaca. Fall pushes squirrels, raccoons, and rodents indoors ahead of winter; spring brings denning mothers looking for chimneys and attic corners; summer is when bat colonies are most visible in older homes and when young animals start ranging on their own. Most Ithaca jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

faqs.q: What does wildlife removal cost in Dryden?
faqs.a: Dryden quotes depend on how much of the property is in play — the farmhouse alone, or the farmhouse plus the barns and sheds where half the animals live. We inspect what you include, explain the priorities, and give you a written figure for removal and screening.

faqs.q: When do Dryden groundhogs do the most damage?
faqs.a: From spring emergence through fall, but the structural damage concentrates where burrows meet buildings — barn foundations, shed floors, and Dryden's many bank barns. Garden losses get the attention; foundation burrows do the expensive harm. Our crew removes the animals and screens the building skirts, then shows you which field-edge systems are worth watching.

Dryden.wildlife_intro:
Dryden is Tompkins County's farming town east of Ithaca — a small village, dairy and crop country, and wooded roads climbing toward Cortland County. Groundhogs set the agenda on the farms and large village lots alike, skunks den under the outbuildings, and the village's older homes draw bats and squirrels. Virgil Creek and Fall Creek's headwaters thread the town, keeping raccoon routes green and busy.

Dryden is unhurried country, and its wildlife problems are usually mature by the time anyone calls: established burrow systems, colonies in farmhouse eaves, skunk families settled for the season. Our crew inspects Dryden properties whole — house and outbuildings — removes the animals, and screens or seals by structure. In farm country the honest job is the property job, and we quote it that way.

Lansing.wildlife_intro:
Lansing runs down Tompkins County's northeast side to Cayuga Lake's eastern shore — farm country inland, lake homes and cottages along the water, and subdivisions growing near the Ithaca edge. The lake properties define its distinctive calls: bats in cottage eaves, raccoons under lake-house decks and in chimneys, and seasonal homes that sit quiet for weeks. Inland, groundhogs and skunks cover the farms as they do everywhere in the county.

Shore and inland split the work in Lansing. Lake homes need crawlspace and deck attention plus the roofline; farm properties need outbuilding screening plus the farmhouse. Our crew inspects by setting, photographs entries for seasonal owners, removes the animals, and seals or screens accordingly — Cayuga's shore concentrates raccoons in summer, when the lake houses are full and the conflicts peak.

faqs.q: Why do Trumansburg porches attract skunks?
faqs.a: The village's raised porches offer dry, dark, dog-proof shelter a few steps from gardens and gorge-edge forage, and skunk mothers choose them every spring. Skunks are a designated rabies-vector species in New York, so an occupied porch is a professional removal. Our crew removes the family and screens the porch perimeter with buried-edge screening that keeps it closed.
